blog.title: How often should you get your windows cleaned in Market Drayton?
blog.excerpt: The honest answer depends more on where you live than most people think — here's how to work out the right frequency for your home.
blog.body:
Most people ask this the wrong way round. They start with "how often do window cleaners usually come" rather than "what does my house actually need" — and end up either paying for cleans they don't need, or waiting so long that grime builds up and takes longer to shift each time.

The honest answer is that frequency depends more on where your house sits than on any general rule. Here's how to actually work it out.

## The standard starting point: every 4 weeks

For most homes in Market Drayton, a 4-weekly clean is the sweet spot. It's frequent enough that dirt never gets a chance to bake onto the glass, and it keeps window frames and sills looking cared for rather than neglected.

## When you might need it more often

- **Near the A53 or another busy road** — traffic grime settles on glass faster than you'd think, especially on ground-floor windows.
- **Under trees, or near farmland** — sap, pollen and dust from nearby fields build up quickly, particularly in spring and during harvest.
- **South or west-facing glass** — more direct sun bakes on rain spots and mineral deposits, making them harder to remove the longer they sit.
- **Commercial premises** — shopfronts get judged daily by passing customers, so weekly or fortnightly is standard.

## When every 6-8 weeks is genuinely fine

- Upper-floor windows with limited direct exposure to the road or trees.
- Homes set back from the road with a sheltered aspect.
- Properties used seasonally, such as holiday lets between bookings.

## What Market Drayton's water means for the result

Local mains water here is classed as hard, which matters more than most people realise. Hard water leaves mineral deposits behind as it dries, which is exactly what causes the streaky, cloudy look people associate with "bad" window cleaning — regardless of how often it's done. Using pure, filtered water avoids this entirely.

## Our honest recommendation

Start at 4-weekly. If your windows still look genuinely clean right up until the next visit, stretch to 6 or 8 weeks and save a little. If they're looking tired again within two weeks, that's a sign your property's exposure calls for a shorter cycle.

blog.title: Hard water and streaky windows: why it happens and what actually helps
blog.excerpt: Market Drayton's mains water is classed hard — here's what that means for your glass, and why pure water cleaning solves it properly.
blog.body:
If your windows look streaky within days of being cleaned, the problem usually isn't the cleaning — it's the water. Market Drayton's mains supply, provided by Severn Trent, is classed as hard water.

## What "hard water" actually means

Hard water carries dissolved minerals, mainly calcium and magnesium, picked up as it passes through the ground before reaching your taps. Those minerals don't evaporate along with the water — they stay behind on any surface the water dries on, glass included.

## Why this ruins a traditional window clean

Traditional window cleaning — a squeegee, some detergent, and tap water — rinses the glass with exactly the water that's causing the problem. Even a perfectly executed clean will dry to a faint white haze or streak pattern as the hard water evaporates and leaves its mineral content behind.

## Why pure water solves it properly

Pure water window cleaning uses water that's been filtered to remove essentially all dissolved minerals before it ever touches your glass. Because there's nothing left in the water to leave a residue, it dries completely clear with no streaking, no matter how hard the water was to begin with.

## What this means for you

- If your current window cleaner still uses tap water and a squeegee, hard water like ours in Market Drayton will always limit how good the finish can be.
- Pure water cleaning isn't a premium extra — for a hard water area, it's the baseline for a genuinely streak-free result.
- It also means frames and sills come out cleaner, since there's no mineral film left behind either.

Every DEC clean uses pure water for exactly this reason.

blog.title: From a Ladder and a Bucket at 18, to DEC Today
blog.excerpt: Long before DEC existed, I was up ladders with a bucket and a chamois at 18 years old. Here's what traditional window cleaning taught me — and why I do it differently now.
blog.body:
I cleaned my first window for money when I was 18. No pure water system, no water-fed pole — just a bucket, a squeegee, a chamois leather, and a ladder against the wall.

If you've never done it the old way, it's harder than it looks. You're carrying a full bucket up a ladder, working out how to reach the top corner of a bay window without overbalancing, and doing it all over again at the next house. In winter your hands go numb before you're halfway down the street. In summer the glass dries before you've finished wiping it, and you're chasing streaks the whole way round.

I did that round for 3 years around Lymington in Hampshire, mostly knocking on doors, mostly collecting cash on the day, mostly working around whatever the weather decided to do that morning. It taught me a few things that have stuck with me:

## What traditional window cleaning actually teaches you

You learn to read a property fast. Every house is a slightly different puzzle — awkward angles, conservatories, windows above a porch roof you can't get a ladder near. You work it out or you don't get paid.

You learn what customers actually care about. Not one person ever asked me about the brand of squeegee I used. They cared about turning up when I said I would, doing a proper job, and not making a mess of their flower beds with the ladder.

You learn the limits of the old way. Ladders against a house are a genuine safety risk, for you and for the property. Tap water leaves streaks no matter how good your technique is, especially anywhere with hard water. And cash on the doorstep means someone has to be in, has to have the right notes, and has to remember it's cleaning day in the first place.

## Why DEC does it differently now

Years on, coming back to window cleaning with DEC, I didn't want to just repeat what I did at 18. The trade's moved on, and so have I.

That's the whole reason DEC runs the way it does:

- Pure water instead of a bucket and chamois — no streaks, whatever the water's like locally, and a proper finish on frames and sills, not just the glass.
- A water-fed pole instead of a ladder — safer for me, safer for your property, and it reaches upstairs windows a ladder never could without me being balanced on your flower bed.
- A text the day before, not a knock and hope you're in — the bit of the old job that always felt most unreliable, fixed properly.
- Card or Direct Debit instead of cash on the day — nobody has to remember to leave money out, and I'm not carrying cash round the estate.

Everything I do at DEC now is built to fix the actual weak points of how I used to do this job at 18 — not because the old way didn't work, but because I've had years since then to work out what a genuinely reliable service looks like from the customer's side, not just the cleaner's.

If you've had window cleaners before who didn't turn up when they said, or left streaks no matter how hard they scrubbed — that's exactly the gap DEC was built to close.

blog.title: Can you clean windows in the rain? Why pure water still works
blog.excerpt: Seen us cleaning in the drizzle and wondered if it's worth it? Here's why pure water cleaning still works when it rains, and when we'll stop.
blog.body:
"Are you really cleaning windows in the rain?" It's one of the questions we get asked most, usually with a slightly worried look. It's a fair question. For years the rule was that a rainy day meant a wasted window clean. With pure water cleaning that rule doesn't really apply any more, and here's why.

## Why rain used to ruin a window clean

Traditional window cleaning uses soapy water, a scrubber and a squeegee. If rain lands on glass that's just been done that way, it lands on a thin film of detergent. The drops pick up that residue and dry as marks.

Worse, the frames and sills usually don't get cleaned properly with a squeegee. When it rains, the dirt sitting on them gets washed straight down onto the freshly cleaned glass.

So the problem was never really the rain. It was what the rain landed on.

## What makes the marks: the dirt, not the water

When water dries on glass, anything dissolved or floating in it gets left behind. That's what you see as spots and streaks: dust, pollen, traffic grime, and minerals from hard tap water.

Rain itself is fairly clean when it falls. The marks you see on windows after a shower mostly come from the dirt the rain picks up on its way down the glass, the frames and the window above.

## How pure water cleaning is different

We clean with water that has been filtered to remove almost everything dissolved in it, including the minerals in Market Drayton's hard mains water. A soft brush on a water-fed pole scrubs the glass, the frames and the sills, then everything gets a thorough rinse.

That gives you three things that matter on a wet day:

- **No soap left on the glass.** There's no film for rain to mix with, so drops have nothing to leave behind.
- **The frames and sills are clean too.** Rain running off them later doesn't carry dirt back down onto the glass.
- **The glass is left rinsed and clean.** Rain that lands afterwards is landing on clean glass, so it dries with very little to show.

In fact, a clean window that gets rained on usually looks better afterwards than a dirty one, because there's nothing for the rain to stick to.

## Is it ever too wet to clean?

Light rain and drizzle aren't a problem, and we'll keep working through them. There are a few times we will stop or rearrange your clean, though:

- **Lightning nearby.** Water-fed poles often contain carbon fibre, which conducts electricity, and a long wet pole is the last thing you want to hold up in a thunderstorm.
- **Strong winds.** A long pole in a gusty wind isn't safe for us or for your property.
- **Frost and ice.** Water freezing on the glass or on paths is a safety issue, so on very cold mornings we'll start later or come back another day.
- **Very heavy downpours.** If we can't see the glass clearly, we can't check it's properly clean, so we'll wait for it to ease off.

If the weather means we need to move your clean, we'll let you know. You already get a text the day before every visit.

## What about the occasional marks?

We'll be honest: now and then you might see faint marks after heavy rain. That happens when the rain carries a lot of dust, for example after a dry spell or when there's dust in the air from far away. Those marks show on every window on the street, cleaned or not, and they come off easily at your next clean.

## The bottom line

Cleaning windows in the rain with pure water isn't cutting corners. It's how the method is designed to work. Keeping to your schedule whatever the weather means your windows never get the chance to build up grime, which is what really makes glass look tired.
